# Purpose and scope

This document explains how ratpackR was run in a Claude Code cloud session and reviewed for
bugs: what was asked at each step, how Claude Code responded, and how the bug review and the
fix testing were carried out.

ratpackR is André Punt's R management strategy evaluation (MSE) framework ("NewRat"),
applied to SESSF stocks. Each simulated year, an operating model (OM) projects one or more
stocks; an estimation model (EM), usually Stock Synthesis (SS), is fitted; and a harvest
control rule sets RBCs and TACs.

I forked the code to a personal public repository, `paulburch/ratpackR`. The project had two
aims:

1. **run ratpackR on Linux** in a cloud session (it had only ever been run on Windows);
2. **review the code for correctness bugs**, then test whether fixing each bug on its own
   breaks other parts of the code.

The whole project ran in one Claude Code cloud session, an isolated Linux container
(Ubuntu 24.04, 4 cores). I gave the instructions; Claude Code did the work and pushed the
results to GitHub. **Nothing was pushed to André's repository** (`puntae/ratpackR`), and
André's model code was changed only on separate branches, with each change kept minimal.

## Where the results are

| Branch | Contents |
|---|---|
| `linux-portability` | Linux set-up (`setup_linux.sh`, `docs/cloud_setup.md`), portable paths, the platform-dependent SS call, and a smoke-test script. Pull request #1 into the fork's `main`. |
| `bug-review` | the above plus `docs/bug_review.md` (the bug review) and `docs/bug_checks.R` (reproducible checks) |
| `bugfix-experiments` | the above plus one commit per tested fix, the running log `docs/bugfix/bugfix_log.md`, the rebuilt parallel driver, and a regression test suite (`tests/run_all.sh`) |

# The initial request

My initial prompt set out the background and the task. Its main points were:

> ratpackR is André Punt's R MSE framework for SESSF fish stocks. Paul Burch (CSIRO) forked
> it to `paulburch/ratpackR` (public, personal GitHub account) … Paul works on Windows; the
> code has never been run on Linux. Goals: make it runnable in the cloud, then do a bug review
> that Paul will go through afterwards. The fork is public, so nothing confidential or
> AFMA-sourced goes in. Keep changes to André's files minimal so upstream merges stay clean.
>
> **Part 1: get it running on Linux.** Install R, a C++ toolchain for `Rcpp::sourceCpp`, and
> `r4ss`, `RTMB`, `Rcpp`, `RcppArmadillo` as a repeatable `setup_linux.sh`, documented in
> `docs/cloud_setup.md`. Make the hard-coded `setwd("C:/Research/NewRat/...")` paths portable
> (for example `Sys.getenv("RATPACK_ROOT", unset = getwd())`) and fix case-sensitivity
> mismatches. Make the Stock Synthesis call platform-dependent so that Linux uses
> `CodeBase/ss3_linux`, and report its version. Smoke-test Silver.warehou with the fewest
> simulations and projection years, first without estimation (`Estimation.test <- 1`), then
> with estimation. Keep `Results/` and `Temp/` out of git.
>
> **Part 2: bug review.** Review `RatpackR.R` and `R Inserts/` for wrong indexing, off-by-one
> errors, misuse of `<<-`, divide-by-zero or NaN, overwritten results (for example `Buffer` in
> `SetBuffer`), and drift in `R Inserts/Parallel/`. Where possible confirm each suspected bug
> with a small reproducible R check. Write `docs/bug_review.md` ranked by severity, with
> `file:line`, trigger, effect, suggested fix, and confirmed or suspected. **Don't change
> André's code to fix the bugs; only report them.**
>
> Done means: the branch is pushed, and the final message lists what ran, what failed (with
> errors), run times and every change made to the original files.

The repository's `CLAUDE.md` file, which Claude Code reads automatically, added standing
rules: commit under my personal GitHub identity, never push to upstream, keep the diffs
against André's files small, and keep confidential data out of the public fork.

# How the work progressed: prompts and responses

## Part 1: getting ratpackR running on Linux

**What Claude Code did.**

- **Software installation.** The cloud network policy blocked CRAN and r-universe. Claude
  Code installed R 4.5.3, the compilers and the binary packages from conda-forge (via
  micromamba), and built RTMB 2.0 and r4ss 1.56.0 from GitHub. The CRAN `r4ss` is now only a
  stub that points to GitHub. All of this is scripted in `setup_linux.sh` and takes about
  3.5 minutes.
- **Portability changes**, all small, with Windows behaviour unchanged:
  - run streams take their root from `RATPACK_ROOT` instead of the hard-coded
    `C:/Research/...` path;
  - file-name case mismatches were fixed (`RatPackR.r`, `R inserts/Readin.R` and others);
  - on Linux the SS executable is copied into each EM folder as `ss3`, so SS writes the
    `ss3.par` file the code expects.
- **Stock Synthesis version.** `ss3_linux` reports **SS V3.30.26.00, safe build, ADMB 13.2**.
- **Missing inputs.** The Silver.warehou OM and EM files are missing from `Inputs CSIRO/`, in
  the fork and upstream alike. The complete set in `Inputs Buffer/` was used instead.
- **Smoke tests** (1 simulation, 1 projection year), all completed:

| `Estimation.test` | Time | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (no estimation) | 78 s | SS read back all 147 `.par` values exactly |
| 2 (deterministic data, SS estimation) | 88 s | 42 parameters estimated, maximum gradient 1.8e-5 |
| 99 (real, stochastic data) | 95 s | 42 parameters estimated, maximum gradient 2.9e-5 |

**Response to me.** Claude Code reported the above, flagged the missing input files, and
noted that the first push had failed: the Claude GitHub app had no write access to the
repository. It supplied the work as a git patch in the meantime.

## Getting the work onto GitHub

| My prompt (paraphrased) | Response |
|---|---|
| "Suggest further actions for this cloud session." | A prioritised list: fix GitHub access and push; obtain the missing CSIRO inputs; test the most important bugs; run all stocks; draft a note to André. |
| "I think I have done #1, could you please check." | Push still refused, so Claude Code diagnosed it: reads worked but writes returned "Resource not accessible by integration", meaning the app was not installed on the repository. It gave the GitHub settings steps. |
| "I installed Claude on my GitHub, could you check again." | Push succeeded. |
| (a stop hook repeatedly asked for the commits to be re-authored under Claude's identity) | Declined, because `CLAUDE.md` requires my identity. Confirmed later: commits stay under my GitHub noreply address, not my personal email, to keep it out of a public repository. |

## Decisions on the next phase

I asked for the list of items needing my attention, and then decided:

> #1 commit as paulburch … #2 do I need a branch for Linux? If I do, make this and do the pull
> request. #3 For bugs I want to explore whether fixing any of them individually causes other
> parts of the code to break; can you do it sequentially with tests. Before you start this,
> please write a file to the git repo that describes all of the bugs you found. #4 [the
> `FixedCosts` bug] is likely a placeholder for a feature in development; add this
> qualification to the bug report.

**Response:**

- the work was split into the `linux-portability` and `bug-review` branches, with pull
  request #1;
- the `FixedCosts` qualification was added to the bug report;
- fixes were applied one at a time on `bugfix-experiments` (method in Section 4.3).

I then asked whether Claude Code could continue while my machine was closed. It can: the
session runs in the cloud, and work continues while a request is being processed. I asked it
to *"continue with the low severity items then the suspected items"*. Later, from its list of
suggestions, I asked it to do *"4 and 5"*: finish the open items (the parallel version,
`CatchType` 3 and the Tier 4a P.cod result), and add a regression test script.

# How the bug check was done

## Step 1: reading the code

Claude Code read the whole engine and its modules, about 10 000 lines:

- `RatpackR.R` (projection, harvest control rules, TAC adjustment, multispecies F solver,
  reference points);
- `R Inserts/ReadIn.R`, `Assessment.R` (SS input writing, Tiers 1a, 4a, 4b and 5), `DataGen.R`,
  `WriteOut.R` and `SaveFiles.R`;
- `Model.cpp` and `Utils.cpp`;
- the `R Inserts/Parallel/` copies, compared line by line with the main versions.

For each function it looked for the classes of error in the brief. It also compared related
routines with each other: the equilibrium age structure against the projection's movement
convention, and what the input writers produce against what the readers expect.

## Step 2: confirming suspected bugs with reproducible checks

Claude Code wrote `docs/bug_checks.R`, which loads the real functions and a copy of the
Silver.warehou inputs and runs 20 checks in about 30 seconds. Each prints CONFIRMED or NOT
REPRODUCED. The checks used three kinds of evidence:

- **calling the real functions** with controlled inputs. For example, `SetBuffer` with a
  default buffer of 0.8 returned an unchanged TAC, and `SPR_ref` with one-way movement put no
  fish in the receiving area;
- **edited input copies.** For example, a different catch-bias row for fleet 2 was ignored,
  and a positive steepness bias didn't reach the SS control file;
- **evidence from the smoke runs.** For example, the per-area discard output was 0 while
  total discards were 6 792 t, and Cost and Profit were NA in every output file.

In addition, the SS `.par` file round-trip and the age-error matrix orientation were
checked; both are correct.

## Step 3: the bug report

The findings are in `docs/bug_review.md`: **24 bugs ranked High, Medium or Low, plus 21
suspected issues**. Each has its location (`file:line`), what triggers it, what goes wrong,
a suggested fix, and its status (confirmed by test, confirmed by inspection, or suspected).
The most important were:

- **`SetBuffer` never applied the default buffer.** The buffer-study input
  (`Inputs Buffer/Silver.warehou.EM`, default 0.9) was affected.
- **`FixedCosts` was read from a non-existent column**, so Cost and Profit were NA. This is
  probably a feature still in development.
- **The SS folder clean-up could never run**, leaving about 11 MB per assessment.
- **Multi-stock errors:** the TAC reallocation loop used the wrong variable (`Istocks`), and
  PGMSY divided by zero.
- **Multi-area errors** in the reference-point and initial-equilibrium routines.
- **Several crash paths:** discard-age data, Tier 5 runs, one Tier 4a option and closed areas.
- **Drift:** the `Parallel/` code was an outdated copy of the engine.

## Step 4: testing fixes one at a time

To answer my question, *does fixing a bug on its own break anything else?*, each fix was
handled the same way:

1. **One commit per fix** on `bugfix-experiments`, applied cumulatively in severity order,
   changing only the lines needed. André's original code remains untouched on the other
   branches.
2. **The same tests after every fix:**
   - all 20 checks, where only the fixed bug's check should change;
   - the smoke runs at `Estimation.test` 1 and 2 (and 99 where relevant);
   - a comparison of every output file with the previous step, value by value, at a
     relative tolerance of 1e-8.

   A repeat run of the unfixed code gave identical output, so any difference could be
   attributed to the fix.
3. **Edited input copies for code the standard runs never reach.** These included discard
   ages, conditional age-at-length, Tier 5, Tier 4a with other settings, equilibrium catch,
   closed areas, implementation error and invalid settings. Each was run on the old and the
   new code.
4. **A log entry for every step** in `docs/bugfix/bugfix_log.md`, pushed after each fix, so
   the work could continue after an interruption.

## Results

| Group | Outcome | Broke anything else? |
|---|---|---|
| High and Medium bugs (#1–#18) | 17 fixed and tested; parallel drift (#17) rebuilt later | No |
| Low bugs (#19–#24) | all 6 fixed and tested | No |
| Suspected items (#25–#45) | 14 fixed and tested; 6 left unchanged by decision (harmless, intended, or need André); Tier 4a P.cod investigated | No |
| Open items (#15, #17, #45) | `CatchType` 3 input F restored; parallel driver rebuilt; Tier 4a P.cod explained | No |

- **No fix broke another part of the code.** Every run completed, and outputs changed only
  where a fix was meant to act. With all fixes applied together, the deterministic RBCs were
  unchanged.
- **The 2026 TAC fell by exactly the 0.9 buffer** that is now applied (6 727 → 6 054 t in
  the no-estimation run).
- **Stochastic runs draw different random numbers** after the random-seed fix, so they can't
  be compared draw-for-draw with older runs.
- **One suspected item was a real crash:** closing an area stopped the run.
- **The Tier 4a RBC of 0 for P.cod comes from the input settings, not the code.** The model
  assumes biomass in 1985–1995 averaged BMSY (40% of unfished), whereas in the OM the stock
  was at 85–132% of unfished in those years. Its non-convergence in early tests was caused by
  noise-free test data.
- **The rebuilt parallel driver** reproduces the serial run exactly (2 simulations, all
  output files identical).

## Step 5: a regression test suite

`tests/run_all.sh` runs the checks, the Silver.warehou runs with and without estimation, and
a P.cod Tier 4a run, and compares them with stored reference outputs. The standard set takes
about 4 minutes; `--full` adds the stochastic and parallel runs (about 9 minutes). It passes
on the current code and detects a change of 4 × 10⁻⁵ in a single value. It is meant to be
run after each merge of André's updates.

# Decisions for André

- whether the default and time buffers combine multiplicatively (#2);
- the PGMSY rule for a linked fleet with no recent catch (#5);
- the movement age convention (#8);
- a TAC of 0 when there is no TAC management (Tier 5, #14);
- whether reference points should use current-year M (#31);
- the environmental-index condition (#38), insurance and predator modules (#41, #42);
- multi-area mapping of F and initial values;
- the `CatchType` 3 restriction (no depletion tuning) and the zero F in the last two years
  of the `.SAV` file;
- P.cod Tier 4a anchor years;
- whether `R Inserts/Parallel/Assessment.R`, now unused, can be deleted.

# Lessons for using Claude Code on similar projects

- **State constraints explicitly.** For example: a public fork, so no confidential data;
  minimal diffs against upstream; and how to treat the original author's code. A
  `CLAUDE.md` file in the repository keeps such rules in force across sessions.
- **Ask for evidence, not opinions.** Requiring a reproducible check for each suspected bug
  separated real bugs from false alarms, and turned up one crash that inspection alone had
  rated as suspected.
- **Change one thing at a time and compare outputs.** Cumulative single fixes, each
  regression-tested against the previous step, show exactly what each change does.
- **Keep a running log in the repository.** Cloud sessions are temporary; a log pushed after
  each step makes the work resumable and reviewable.
- **Check access early.** GitHub write access for the Claude app, and network access for
  package repositories, were the main practical obstacles. Both were solved by settings
  changes, not code.
